evidence: Hor. S. 2.4.18: nē gallīna malum respōnset dūra palātō
terms.comment: Horace’s word for a tough chicken; its opposite is tener, which he uses of the same bird made tender. Latin has no word that praises a chewy texture as English can; for that, see lentus.

phrases.latin: Haec carō dūra est; diū mandenda.
phrases.english: This meat is chewy; you have to chew it a long time.

phrases.latin: sī vespertīnus subitō tē oppresserit hospes, nē gallīna malum respōnset dūra palātō, doctus eris vīvam mustō mersāre Falernō: hoc teneram faciet.
phrases.english: if a guest descends on you suddenly in the evening, and you don’t want a tough chicken to fight back against his palate, you will have learnt to drown it alive in Falernian must: that will make it tender.

phrases.latin: ita istaec nimis lenta vincla sunt ēscāria: quam magis extendās, tantō adstringunt artius
phrases.english: for those chains of food are very tenacious: the more you stretch them, the tighter they hold

sources: Lewis & Short: durus · Lewis & Short: lentus
